text: It may be objected that the chapter merely follows the economy of ancient narrative, which rarely reports the feelings of its persons, and never explains either feeling or motive; and the objection may in part be allowed. But the narrator elsewhere tells what persons feel: Esau cries out, Jacob is afraid, Joseph weeps. He is not here ignorant of his own method. Restraint, in this narrator's voice, works as a kind of accusation; the reticence of Genesis 22 is deliberate.
